title: 'I started in my 20s and made £8,000': Why women are often better investors than men
description: Image source, Teleri EvansImage caption, Teleri Evans used her investments to put a deposit down on her first homeByWill SmalePhil Leake and Jess Carr
body: Image source, Teleri EvansImage caption, Teleri Evans used her investments to put a deposit down on her first homeByWill SmalePhil Leake and Jess CarrBBC NewsWomen who invest their money get slightly higher long-term returns than men, new analysis suggests.But only about a quarter of UK women have investments, compared with about 40% of men, a separate report shows.We've looked at the data behind these trends, which reveal some surprising differences in how men and women approach investing.Teleri Evans was 25 when she began saving into a Help To Buy ISA then a couple of years later she took out a stocks and shares Lifetime ISA. By 33, she had £40,000 saved - with £8,000 of it returns on her investments."I saved aggressively, and lived at my mum's for half of that time, so I could save as close as possible to the maximum £4,000 per year into Lifetime ISA," she says.The civil servant from Cardiff used the money towards a house deposit earlier this year with her partner.Only 26% of UK women invest, but that this falls to 23% for those under 45, according to a study by consumer finance website Boring Money. In contrast, 41% of all men invest, which holds steady at 40% of those under 45.So why are fewer women investing than men?It can be "largely attributed to culture", according to Gillian Fleming, co-founder and managing director of UK-based Mint Ventures, a women-led angel investment firm."Men historically have been more likely to make family investment decisions, and women have also historically not owned the balance of wealth, but that is changing now," she says."Also, money and wealth creation is not a topic that women often discuss, and we would like to change that."Teleri says she has noticed a shift of late. "Investing is definitely something that women are talking about more, which is always a good thing," she says. "That's the case with my friendship group."When women do invest in stocks and shares, analysis by Fidelity International found that over three years its female personal investing customers recorded cumulative returns of 50%, compared with 47% for men. The analysis does not identify the reason for the difference, but why may it be the case?One possible clue to women's slightly higher long-term returns lies in how often they buy and sell their investments, with Barclays data showing that women trade around half as frequently as men.This could be because women are more patient and risk averse, says Joanna Floyd, business psychologist at London-based The Work Psychologists. "Studies show that male investors trade more than women, chasing higher returns, but women actually get higher returns," she says."The restraint that keeps women out of the market in the first place is the very same thing that rewards them once they are in it."That more cautious approach to risk can be seen beyond investing, with women more likely to choose certainty when faced with a financial gamble.When it comes to how women invest, Fleming says they are deliberately more cautious."Women are often accused of being more risk adverse, we call it more risk aware," she says. "Certainly from speaking to male investors their main focus is on the rate of return."Fleming also says women appear to invest more broadly. "Men are more likely to invest in technology companies for their higher potential returns, whereas women want to invest in a broader range, from retail to food and drink, health and beauty, fem tech and creative industries."Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at financial services company Hargreaves Lansdown, agrees that women choose the companies they invest in carefully."Women appear to place relatively greater weight on where their money is going and what impact it might have, as well as the reassurance that an investment is right for them," she says."Our research suggests men are...more readily attracted by the potential financial return."Jemma Slingo, pensions and investment specialist at investment firm Fidelity International, says female investors "appear more likely to connect investing with real-life goals, from building emergency savings to looking after children."It's important to remember women in the UK generally have less money to invest than men because the continuing gender pay gap means they earn less on average.Macdonald says that the investment sector "needs to do a better job of making investing feel accessible, relevant and connected to people's own goals and values"."Addressing this would be good for women's long-term financial resilience and for the UK economy."Women who invest

title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
description: New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to stop betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving hig
body: New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to stop betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and "for many people, the high streets they grew up with have become unrecognisable".BBC News has exposed organised crime on high streets across the country, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes and vapes, selling cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".The plans announced by the government include:Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco or up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least £1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.Burnham said "the rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services, and community spaces that people are crying out for".He added: "That's not on. I said we would improve Britain's high streets, and that's exactly what we are starting to do."We're putting communities back in control and giving local people a real say over what opens on their high street."In response to the announcement, Conservative shadow communities secretary Sir James Cleverly said "once-treasured shops" have been replaced by a "smattering of rogue operators".But Sir James said increases to business rates by Labour had left "empty units for whoever is left standing to fill".He said: "Unless the government takes steps to support the high streets and hard-working businesses, Labour's increases in planning regulation will just mean more empty and boarded up shops."For the Liberal Democrats, home affairs spokesman Max Wilkinson said Burnham's plan "could go up in a puff of smoke" unless he toughens up powers to "properly crack down on cowboy vape shops and dodgy operators".His calls included asking the prime minister to scrap the business rates system.Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Until this government scraps the jobs tax, addresses sky-high business rates and provides real, fundamental support for high street businesses, this policy will only create even more empty shops on our high streets."A Green Party spokesperson said the government's proposals "look like more inadequate tinkering and reannouncements".They called on the prime minister to "go further and allow councils to introduce rent controls for small businesses". The Betting and Gaming Council said it supports "tough action against criminal operator" and agrees "local people should have a proper say over their high streets".A spokesperson for the industry body added it was "simply wrong" to suggest that betting shops are spreading "unchecked", adding around 3,000 shops have closed since 2019.Councillor Eamonn O'Brien, who chairs the Local Government Association, said it was "positive" that councils and communities "will get a greater say on what shops and services are found on their high streets".For 18 months, BBC News has reported on high street organised crime, including drug gangs, money laundering, child sexual exploitation reports, immigration crime and ghost directors linked to shop fronts selling illegal cigarettes and illegal vapes.In April 2025, the BBC joined the NCA as it raided barbers, mini-marts and vape shops in response to growing intelligence reports that some of these shops were being used for money laundering and illegal working.In May and June of last year, the team found secret underground tunnels supplying sacks of illegal cigarettes to high street mini-marts in Hull.In July last year, mass Freedom of Information requests revealed for the first time that 3,700 illegal shops had operated across the UK.In November, the BBC exposed asylum seekers buying and selling high street mini-marts for cash and criminal kingpins erasing £60,000 illegal working fines, and revealed a Kurdish organised crime gang operating on high streets the length of Britain.In response, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood launched an "urgent" investigation led by the NCA, Immigration Enforcement, HMRC and police forces from across the country. She said the BBC's evidence proved that "the system was broken" and demonstrated a pull factor in the small boat crisis.In March the BBC revealed a senior council worker had repeatedly shared with West Midlands authorities reports of children as young as 11 being sexually abused in high street mini-marts, and last month undercover reports exposed how cocaine, cannabis, laughing gas and prescription pills were being offered for sale.One street visited in the West Midlands was described as "lawless" by an anonymous law enforcement source.After the report, six mini-marts and vape shops on one high street in Cradely Heath, Sandwell were forced to close following an investigation by police and Trading Standards.Earlier this year, ministers announced a £30m enforcement operation targeting high street businesses suspected of money laundering, tax evasion and illegal working. Raids involving police, HMRC, Trading Standards and Immigration Enforcement have since taken place across the country.Additional reporting by Phill Edwards and Richard Wheeler

title: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots
description: US President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MM
body: US President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) shots."Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today," Trump said. "In those times, people were much healthier and of course the high rates of autism now observed did not exist."The president has long cast doubt on the safety of MMR vaccines, but multiple studies have found no connection between the shots and autism.The order also recommends that the number of childhood vaccines drop to 11 from the existing 18 recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).Trump's order serves as guidance, not a mandate, since shots required for school attendance are set at the state level, rather than by the federal government.Speaking in the Oval Office on Monday, the president said his administration "is recognising gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases".The immunisations recommended for all children under the order are for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella or chicken pox."We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor."The president suggested the MMR vaccine could be "quite lethal" if given at once. He compared it to pouring a bottle of soda into a child's body.When a reporter asked for evidence of the "lethal" claim, Trump said: "What I've heard is that there are some people that say it is that way."According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), external, the MMR vaccine carries a very small risk of febrile seizures for young children. Those with health issues, including severe allegeric reactions or weakened immune systems, are advised to consult with healthcare providers before taking the shots.The agency says "most people who get MMR vaccine do not have any serious problems with it", and that getting the vaccine "is much safer than getting measles, mumps, or rubella".According to the CDC, there is "no published scientific evidence that shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots". Experts say that allowing time between jabs means children are more likely to contract diseases in the interim or that they are more likely to miss appointments if there are multiple shots.Trump's Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F Kennedy Jr said the proposed changes were meant to give parents choice, not prohibit access to childhood vaccines.Since taking office in 2025, Kennedy has sought to change and loosen vaccine regulations. During a tense 20-minute interview on CNN last week, Kennedy insisted he had "never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine".Trump administration officials have said the order means children in the US would receive much less than the 72 shots recommended under the previous vaccine schedule, a figure that assumes annual flu and Covid-19 doses.Dr Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said Trump's executive order was "dangerous" and not based on "gold-standard science"."Delaying or skipping shots is risky, especially as measles continues to spread and children go back to school," Racine said. Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, who was the deciding vote in the Senate to confirm Kennedy as health secretary, also admonished Trump's executive order on Monday, labelling it "wrong"."The President does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy, a physician, wrote on X. "Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism."Experts fear that if parents refrain from getting their children vaccinated as a result of the discredited idea that childhood vaccines are linked to autism, it risks the re-emergence of diseases like measles.Multiple studies have found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism. A recent high-quality study from Denmark in 2019 looked at 657,461 children and concluded that the data did not support the MMR vaccine causing or triggering autism.On its website, the CDC recommends that two doses of the combined MMR vaccine be given to children, starting with the first dose at 12-15 months and the second between the ages of four and six.How often and how many vaccines children in the US receive is based on the times when vaccines will work best with their immune systems and when they are most vulnerable to certain diseases, according to the AAP.There is no medical reason to delay or skip recommended immunisations, the AAP says.Trump's order also calls for the development of alternatives to aluminium in vaccines, and to test if those alternatives are safer and more effective.But the AAP, external says studies have found no significant health risks associated with the tiny amounts of aluminium salts in vaccines.Small amounts of aluminium salts - which are found naturally in soil, water and foods - have been used in some vaccines for decades in order to boost the body's immune response. That means lesser quantities of the vaccine and fewer doses are needed, according to AAP.

title: Disabled in a heatwave: 'We're talking about survival'
description: Image source, Emily Davison/fashioneyesta2012Image caption, Emily Davison works with a guide dog as she has a visual impairment related to a congenita
body: Image source, Emily Davison/fashioneyesta2012Image caption, Emily Davison works with a guide dog as she has a visual impairment related to a congenital health conditionByMaddie MolloyClimate & Science reporterHeatwaves this summer have brought travel disruption, overheating homes and school closures for millions - and there is a fifth heatwave expected to hit this week.It is well-documented that those with existing health conditions and disabilities are most at risk during extreme heat episodes.But these additional and specific challenges faced - from struggling service dogs to overheating wheelchairs - are often overlooked, even in public advice and emergency planning, say campaigners and researchers."For somebody who is able-bodied, it's uncomfortable but if you identify as disabled, we're starting to talk about survival," said campaigner Doug Paulley.Emily Davison says soaring temperatures force her to put the welfare of her guide dog, Rosie, before her own independence."The dog's health has to come first," Davison said.Davison is a London-based journalist and content creator, but heatwaves have forced her to cancel journeys to events because it is often too hot for Rosie to travel safely - missing out on potential earnings.Public transport like buses often overheat and she avoids Uber after "too many experiences where they've not let me in with a dog".She says finding available taxis has become more difficult, even with London Taxicard scheme, a subsidised taxi service for people with mobility impairments or severe sight loss.Davison says every trip now requires careful planning, which can make her feel isolated and limits both her work and independence."It does put the brakes on your life," she said. "When you're in this situation and you've got a guide dog and you can't do anything, it does make certain things grind to a halt."She is now spending long periods working from home - but says she is lucky to be still able to do this but not all disabled people can."I think the culture of being able to work from home and have that option is really important to keep ensuring that disabled people can still be in employment," Davison said.Image source, Jimmy Macfarlane/@jimmy.mac01Image caption, Jimmy Macfarlane uses a wheelchair - when lifts break down in the heat it can leave him strandedJimmy Macfarlane is a Cardiff-based actor who needs to travel for his job - but he uses a powered wheelchair.During this summer's heatwaves people have taken to social media to report phone batteries draining faster because of the high temperatures, but for Jimmy those batteries are what get him around."The heat definitely impacts the chair and it makes the battery go down a lot quicker… I always have to think is there a way I can get to where I need to be without moving the chair?" Macfarlane said.Some days he has not even been able to leave his home - he previously lived in a sixth-floor flat and the heat caused the lift to break down.Such problems have been reported in other high-rise buildings by BBC News, but unlike other residents Jimmy cannot just use the stairs to get round the problem."There were times where I was stuck in the flat [for days] until it was fixed," he said.And the heat inside his flat became difficult to manage. Because of his cerebral palsy, everyday tasks already require more energy. "Things like getting changed, having a shower… everything I do takes twice as long as a non-disabled person," he said. "On a hot day, it's even more exhausting."Cooling tricks can be dangerous when blindCommon advice for dealing with the heat is to conserve energy and stay cool by keeping your curtains closed and opening the windows when it is cool.But for Claire Sisk, a content creator and advocate who has distorted vision, this can be dangerous."If I've got all my windows and doors open, I feel incredibly vulnerable because I can't see if anybody is walking into my property. So I have to have them all closed, which is quite unbearable," Sisk said.Image source, Claire Sisk/canseecantsee_Image caption, Claire Sisk gradually lost her sight after suffering two strokes in 2009 when she was aged 29Other measures intended to keep homes cool can introduce new risks. Fans, for example, can become trip hazards because they are not part of her usual layout.When she leaves home, the current weather can make her remaining vision far less reliable. "[When] that sunlight comes out, then that bit of vision just goes," Sisk said.Hot weather can make travel unpredictable, and access issues can waste valuable time on an already exhausting day. She recalled having to wait at a Tube station because of staff shortages. "That can be a bit frustrating because it takes you two hours then to get home when it should have only taken 45 minutes," she said.The cost burden of a heatwaveHollye Kirkcaldy, a PhD researcher at the University of Bath, studies how extreme heat affects disabled people in the UK, and says these experiences are shared by many across the country."You've got inequalities in urban infrastructure, housing, structural conditions around things like social networks and care. If you put all of those together and then you throw heat in, that's what's disabling," Kirkcaldy said.Her research found that official heatwave guidance often does not reflect disabled people's circumstances, while measures presented as simple can in fact create new barriers. This can reduce independence which harms their mental wellbeing and adds financial pressures, she said. Disabled people can be left unable to work and facing additional outgoings like higher energy costs for round-the-clock cooling. Kirkcaldy said in some cases it can be "a trade-off that nobody should have to make between your health and whether you eat."Image source, Doug PaulleyImage caption, Doug Paulley campaigns on disability rights and accessibility in public policyFor disability campaigner Doug Paulley, who has a number of health conditions which are exacerbated by hot temperatures, the experiences of disabled people during heatwaves point to wider problems in society."Disabled people are always amongst the first against the wall whenever there's a significant crisis of any type in society, and this is no exception," Paulley said.During one heatwave, he cancelled physiotherapy and missed giving evidence to the Covid Inquiry because travelling became unsafe."There was just no way that I could have gone. It was dangerously hot and I would have been really unwell."Moving forward climate change must be factored into how people think about access and support, Emily Davison said. "Climate change is a thing. Summers are only going to get hotter."For Doug, the issue is not only how disabled people cope with extreme weather, but whose experiences are considered when decisions are made about the future."Policy is very much set for them, not with them."

title: At least 132 killed in Colombia's largest  earthquake in years
description: At least 132 people are dead and a state of emergency has been declared after Colombia was hit by one of its largest earthquakes in years.The death to
body: At least 132 people are dead and a state of emergency has been declared after Colombia was hit by one of its largest earthquakes in years.The death toll is likely to rise, with more feared trapped under collapsed buildings. The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) at a depth of 103km (64 miles) in Chocó province, the country's geological service said. It was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia. Many of the deaths have been concentrated in the city of Pereira, in Colombia's coffee-growing region, with surrounding cities and the Valle del Cauca region also hit hard. The epicentre of the quake was near the village of San José del Palmar, in Chocó province, but local mayor León Fabio Marín Moncada said that there had miraculously been no deaths or injuries - despite the roads in and out being damaged. More than 480 people were injured in the quakes, Colombia's Association of Capital Cities wrote in a statement update on Monday. About 55km (34 miles) from the epicenter of the earthquake, the city of Pereira saw some of the worst damage. Videos verified by the BBC show at least one building collapsing in Plaza Bolívar, the city's main square, with scattered debris and dust across the open space where many people had gathered.Local authorities have reported at least 40 people dead in the city's metropolitan area, with 65 collapsed buildings. People are believed to be trapped in 15 of them. A curfew is in place in some parts of the city until 05:00 local time on Tuesday. Thirty-two buildings collapsed in Cali, located about 160km south of Pereira and about 200km from the epicentre.  Dan Cutler, 29, is from London but has been in Colombia for about two months as part of a big trip with his partner, and is currently in Cali. Being woken by the earthquake, he told the BBC:  "I've never experienced anything like it.""We sprinted outside in our pyjamas. There's no major structural damage to the hotel, but there are surface cracks in the walls, and paint and plaster have peeled off," he says.There were also reports of deaths in Manizales, Quibdó, Medellín, across the Chocó and Valle del Cauca regions.At least two people have died in Manizales.Speaking to BBC World Service, Angélica Ávila said she had been staying in a hotel in Manizales. She said as the earthquake hit, cracks appeared in the walls. "Everyone was screaming... I saw dust coming out of the neighbouring buildings, and bricks were falling off the walls," she said.Journalist and meteorologist Luis Felipe Molina, from Manizales, was at home when the earthquake struck - about 150km from the epicentre. He explained that due to previous earthquakes, the city has "very strict seismic-resistant building regulations" - so his building was able to resist the impact. "I have 450 books and only a few were left standing on the shelves. You could hear glass breaking and people screaming," he told BBC Mundo. "It was a terrible and terrifying experience."The country's aviation authority has reported damage at several regional airports, including those in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura.In the capital, Bogotá, trees and traffic lights shook violently, with reports of cracks in buildings but so far none of any serious damage to the city's infrastructure. Tremors were felt as far away as  neighbouring Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama. The quake comes less than two months after twin quakes devastated the north of Venezuela, killing more than 6,300 people.Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella has declared a national disaster situation, creating special powers to react to the emergency, including to reallocate budgets. Having only taken up the role on Friday, the new president is immediately faced with a potentially legacy-defining event. Along with the dead, he confirmed that more than 1,500 homes had been damaged.   As the extent of the damage has begun to emerge, world leaders have come forward to offer support. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it was "closely monitoring" the earthquake, and stood "ready to support", while EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU's Copernicus satellite was being used in the rescue operation. The President of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, sent a message of solidarity to the Colombian people and offered personnel and equipment for rescue efforts.According to the US Geological Survey, an estimated 1.5 million people felt shaking close to magnitude seven.It stated that deep earthquakes, like the one which hit on Monday, are usually less dangerous than earthquakes which break closer to the Earth's surface. But they can release energy in a way which is damaging to buildings, with fewer but potentially stronger aftershocks.

title: European Athletics Championships 2026: Amy Hunt wins 100m gold for GB
description: Amy Hunt had her coming of age moment as she stormed to 100m glory to claim her first senior international title and deliver Britain's first gold meda
body: Amy Hunt had her coming of age moment as she stormed to 100m glory to claim her first senior international title and deliver Britain's first gold medal of the European Athletics Championships.Hunt announced herself on the sport's global stage last year with world 200m silver in Tokyo - the first individual international medal of her senior career.Having backed that up with Commonwealth 100m silver two weeks ago, the 24-year-old would not be denied gold this time in Birmingham."I have had such a string of silvers and I was starting to get a bit fed up with it, so I thought it was time for gold," Hunt, who won in 11 seconds flat, told BBC Sport."My parents gifted me these gold earrings to finally level up, because I wear all-silver jewellery. "They said it was time for gold - they left me that note two nights ago - so it made me quite emotional."It was definitely time for me to come of age here."It was Britain's second medal on the opening day of action after the hosts took silver in the mixed 4x400m relay.Yemi Mary John held off Dutch athlete Myrte van der Schoot on the home straight to bring a British quartet also featuring Ben Jefferies, Charlotte Henrich and Toby Harries home in three minutes 10.47 seconds, behind winners Norway (3:09.62).Hunt's breakthrough individual medal last September was a long time coming, but the early years of her senior career were disrupted by injury as she sought to balance the demands of training with studying for an English Literature degree at Cambridge University.Before those challenging years, Hunt set a women's under-18 200m world record in 2019 - breaking Asher-Smith's British under-20 record in the process - but it would be six years before she managed to improve on that personal best time in her favoured event.Hunt also ruptured her quad muscle in 2022 but, with those setbacks now behind her, continues to make exciting progress under the guidance of coach Marco Airale in Italy's northern city of Padova.Now consistently able to produce personal-best performances, the silverware is beginning to follow - and this golden moment signalled a changing of the guard at the top of British sprinting.Discussing her ambitions before the championships, Hunt quoted High School Musical character Sharpay Evans, who sings a song called "I Want It All" in the film.Full of confidence after breaking the 11-second barrier for the first time earlier this season, she raised her arms in celebration after producing a trademark strong finish which delivered her from fifth to first over the second half of the race."I want it all and I'm someone who doesn't shy away from what she knows she can do," said Hunt."I knew I could come away with gold. I had such a big premonition."Hunt could have as many as three opportunities to add to her tally this week, as se competes in the 200m and both the women's and mixed 4x100m relay events.Typically not the quickest off the blocks at almost six-foot tall, Hunt was seventh in the eight-athlete final after the first 10m.But she held her form superbly to overhaul her rivals and end her wait for gold, just two years after finishing seventh in the previous European final in Rome."I just had such a magical feeling," Hunt said."I've won English Schools here, raced here as a 13, 14-year-old. I just had a feeling that this was going to be my night."My first gold. I think it was definitely time for an upgrade, and I'm now kind of fully established."British record holder Asher-Smith lined up in Birmingham as the defending champion - but the 30-year-old could not force her way into medal contention.Asher-Smith, bidding to win a historic seventh gold and become the joint-most successful athlete in the history of the championships, finished fifth in 11.10, as Poland's Ewa Swoboda (11.02) and Belgian Delphine Nkansa (11.06) completed the podium.Like Hunt, Asher-Smith will have further opportunities to draw level with Croatian discus thrower Sandra Elkasevic and Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen, who earlier won a superb 5,000m gold on his comeback from injury.Both will return to action on Wednesday, when attention turns to the women's 200m medals before the weekend's relays.

title: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA
description: Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the top
body: Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the topic of "protecting" women's sports.The Indiana Fever guard said she had received criticism from people who believed she "hated" transgender people, something she denied.She said she wanted to "extend love" to everyone, but added: "I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."She later doubled down on her comments, saying it was "common sense", external to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports.Her words quickly moved beyond basketball and into a wider political debate in the United States.President Donald Trump expressed his support for Cunningham, while vice-president JD Vance said she was "inspiring".Though the 29-year-old later said she is "not a very political person", her remarks have followed her around the country. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organised at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests.The scale of the debate in the media, online and in politics was striking given no openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA.The WNBA operates under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA), a deal negotiated between the league and its players association (WNBPA), setting rules on matters including player salary caps, revenue sharing, benefits and overall league operations.On player eligibility, the CBA states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA."The WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's comments but league commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week in which she said the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents.In the memo, seen by the Associated Press, external, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league".She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities."However, the lack of detail in the league's eligibility criteria has been brought to light by Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022."If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," he wrote on Instagram, external.Kanter Freedom, who has previously spoken out about human rights violations in China and Turkey, among other issues, added: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices."I'm simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for."A day after Kanter Freedom's 'announcement', Royce White - who made three appearances in the NBA as a player and is now a Republican Senate candidate - said he would also declare for the Draft, adding: "I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball."Whether the vagueness of the rules are by design to leave it open to transgender women or a sign of an oversight that genuinely needs tightening up is not clear.BBC Sport has contacted Cunningham's representatives, the WNBA and WNBPA for comment.Cunningham's comments have become a flashpoint inside a league which has a long history of player activism on issues including race, gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights.The players' association did not mention Cunningham by name when it eventually addressed the debate.In a statement the WNBPA denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" and reaffirmed its commitment to "justice, equity, diversity and inclusion".It called on fans to report abusive behaviour at games and added that it would continue to have "hard" conversations but it "will not be used as political pawns".There is strong feeling on both sides of the argument. Minnesota Lynx head coach and president Cheryl Reeve, who said: "I come from a space of inclusion."The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" T-shirt before Minnesota played Indiana earlier this month and was seen speaking to Cunningham on court before the game.Cunningham later said the pair had exchanged their perspectives and that the conversation ended with "love and respect".Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams said she would welcome a transgender athlete "on my team or against my team, any time".Last month, the WNBA suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton from attending the team's next five home games after an exchange with two fans, who were sat courtside displaying signs thanking Cunningham for "speaking up for girls".Keaton reportedly confronted the teenage fans and admonished them during the game. The Storm have since apologised.As for Cunningham, the attention has increasingly become an unwelcome distraction.Having defended her original comments, she said recently that she now wanted the conversation to return to what was happening on court."I want to get back to basketball, it's always been about basketball" she said, arguing that the standard of play in the WNBA was being overshadowed by issues away from the game.But that may prove difficult, as pressure grows on the league to clarify exactly who is eligible to play.In recent years, many governing bodies in sport have amended their rules about the inclusion of transgender athletes at the elite level, moving more towards restrictions.Athletics, cycling and aquatics, for example, have implemented outright bans on transgender women taking part in women's events.In March, it was announced that the women's category of Olympic sports will be limited to biological females from the LA Olympic Games in 2028.The International Olympic Committee (IOC) says eligibility will be determined by a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test, which would prevent transgender women and those with differences in sexual development (DSD) who have gone through male puberty from competing.In the United States, transgender women and girls are banned from competing in women's sports categories in schools, universities and the grassroots level.That was part of an executive order - titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" - signed by President Trump last year. It does not cover professional sport.

schema.headline: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA

title: New Forest firefighting to continue for days as cars abandoned
description: Figure caption, Watch: Video shows van on fire by side of road near New ForestByIndy Almroth-Wright and Marcus WhiteSouth of EnglandUpdated 1 hour ago
body: Figure caption, Watch: Video shows van on fire by side of road near New ForestByIndy Almroth-Wright and Marcus WhiteSouth of EnglandUpdated 1 hour agoA "devastating" wildfire in the New Forest, in Hampshire, is now under control, but firefighters say they will still be working for several days to come.The wildfire began when a van caught fire on the A31 near Bratley Wood shortly after 17:20 BST on Sunday, forcing motorists to abandon more than 20 vehicles.The area hit by the fire is protected heathland and home to a number of rare species, the New Forest National Park Authority said.Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service on Monday evening asked the public to avoid the area and said it was working "into the night". National Highways said the A31 dual carriageway through the New Forest would remain closed until further notice."We expect to have a significant presence for several days, as we work to protect this beautiful part of the New Forest," said the fire service.Aerial footage of scorched vegetation showed how the fire funnelled outwards in a south-easterly direction as the wind fanned the flames.Smoke from the blaze could be seen drifting across both sides of the Solent, prompting fire to urge people to keep doors and windows shut.New Forest National Park Authority warned the impact on the forest ecosystem and rare species would be severe.Figure caption, Flames spread across New Forest heathland"It's rare heathland, which globally is more rare than rainforest," a spokesperson said."We have the highest concentration of lowland heathland in western Europe and it's internationally protected."It is home to all six UK native reptiles, Dartford warblers, nightjars, insects – it's devastating."Gillie Molland, lead ranger for the park authority, told PA it will take "many years" for the area to recover.Image source, Robert StibyImage caption, Smoke from the fire could be seen for miles around, including from Portsmouth 30 miles (40km) awayLindsey Legg, who was with her husband and three children when they were forced to stop by police and leave their car, said: "We started seeing people abandoning their cars. Women and children were walking with buggies."She told BBC Radio Solent: "Police told us 'you can't go any further'. We realised the fire was going through the field - it was pretty scary."We had to abandon the car and cross the central reservation to get away from the side of the fire. We thought the car was going to go up at one point."Image source, Jehanna StrideImage caption, The fire created a smoke plume visible for milesNational Highways said there was significant damage to the road surface and crash barrier following the fire and oil spillage from the burnt out vehicle.It added there was no estimated time for reopening the road, which is a main tourist route to Dorset and south-west England.Hampshire Fire and Rescue Service, aided by neighbouring services, initially scrambled 26 fire engines and four water carriers after receiving 160 emergency calls.In a statement on Monday afternoon, it said more than 120 firefighters were on the scene, with 10 fire engines and 13 off-road vehicles in attendance.The fire service said an 5-mile (8km) hose had been laid from Hightown Lake, just east of Ringwood, to supply water to crews tackling the blaze.Figure caption, Firefighters arrive at A31 New Forest fire sceneImage source, New Forest PoliceImage caption, The fire spread from the A31 into nearby heathland on Sunday eveningThe fire is beginning to have an effect on the hospitality trade, one cafe owner in the area told the BBC on Monday. "Lyndhurst itself is very quiet today," Jo Cowley said."It's a big tourist road, the A31. I think it probably will affect us for most of the week."There's a lot of HGVs, a lot of vans passing through. We're getting customers in, but it's nowhere near the customers you would expect."We've had deliveries that are two or three hours late. It's gridlock out there."Image source, Andrew Matthews/PA WireImage caption, Smoke can still be seen rising from the fire at the heathlandLong periods of hot and dry weather have seen wildfires break out across the UK this summer. Nottinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service declared a major incident on Sunday as two fires in woodland caused a large emergency response.It comes as drought officials have declared 71.3% of England is now in drought, after the nation recorded its driest July since records began in 1836.The East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs moved into drought status on Monday, joining half of England and the whole of Wales.The National Drought Group – made up of regulators, government officials, water companies and agricultural bodies - made the decision after a meeting on Monday.A total of 45 million people are now living in a drought area in England, with more than 27 million facing water use restrictions.Image caption, Smoke from the fire could be seen rising over the New Forest Get in touchYour Voice

title: PM asks justice secretary to keep PC Harper's killers in jail
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told his justice secretary to find a way to exclude PC Andrew Harper's killers from an early release scheme designed t
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told his justice secretary to find a way to exclude PC Andrew Harper's killers from an early release scheme designed to ease prison overcrowding.Burnham is confident a solution can be found to remove Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, from the government plan, the BBC has been told.Downing Street had earlier warned that it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter from the early release of prisoners.PC Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.Under changes to the Sentencing Act made this year, Cole and Bowers, who were found not guilty of murder, will become eligible for release from custody next January after serving half of their sentences.They are in a category of prisoners - those who have committed certain serious violent or sexual crimes - who until now would have had to serve at least two-thirds of their sentence in jail before being considered for release.It is not yet clear how the government will prevent Cole and Bowers from being treated the same as other prisoners with similar sentences.If ministers said, for example, that prisoners with manslaughter convictions could not be considered for the scheme, that would have an instant impact on many other inmates.A government spokesperson told the BBC: "The prime minister has asked the Justice Secretary to work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of PC Harper."A source said the Justice Secretary Alex Norris would set out "in due course" how the government would exclude Cole and Bowers from early release.The prime minister has been making daily calls while on holiday to find a solution, sources told the BBC.Around 5,000 people are expected to be released under the sentencing changes, down from 6,000 after exemptions were previously announced for those convicted of the most serious crimes including rape, child sex offences and grooming.The third man jailed for the manslaughter of PC Harper - the vehicle driver Henry Long - was given a longer 16-year jail term. Because he received what is called an extended determinate sentence at the time, he cannot be considered for this early release scheme.PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, has been among a growing number calling for Cole and Bowers to be denied early release. She and PC Harper had been married for just a month when he was killed in the line of duty.Lissie Harper previously led a successful campaign for Harper's Law, which introduced mandatory life sentences for anyone convicted of killing an emergency worker whilst committing a crime.Former police dog handler Chris Bushnell, who was at the scene of PC Harper's death, said he was "shaking" when he heard that two of the officer's killers might be released early from prison.Bushnell was waiting in a lay-by near Sulhamstead, west Berkshire, in August 2019 when the teenagers' vehicle appeared, dragging PC Harper along the ground.The former constable gave chase until he was ordered to stop and remain where he was. He said: "I've seen people die before. I've seen suicides. This was beyond brutal. It was awful.""To think they could be released early is absolutely outrageous," Bushnell said."I'm angry with them, but I'm also angry with the government. They're spitting in the face of police officers."Aileen O'Connor, chairwoman of Thames Valley Police Federation, added: "The public are speaking loudly and clearly. They agree with us that the government are firmly on the wrong side of this."About 900,000 people have signed O'Connor's petition to stop the killers' early release.But ministers have said prison spaces might run out as soon as October.Dame Vera Baird, a former victims' commissioner, told BBC Two's Newsnight that one "good thing" the government has done is invest money in victim support services, as there would be many people currenty concerned that their attackers will be walking the streets sooner than they had expected.She said the government "need to look at the right people to be letting out more carefully than they've managed so far". Dame Vera added that women and people jailed under controversial Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences could also be considered for early release to alleviate pressure on prisons.IPP sentences were introduced in 2005 and allowed judges to give out sentences with no maximum tariff to perpetrators of serious crimes or repeat offenders.The sentences were scrapped in 2012, but were not retrospectively applied. As of this year, more than 2,000 people are still in prison on IPP sentences according to the United Nations (UN),, external who have called for the end of IPP sentences."I think somebody has to just seize the thing and get it sorted," Dame Vera said. "There has to be a wholesale resentencing attempt, I think, and really that does need thinking through."

title: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
description: Figure caption, Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scamsByLaura BickerChina correspondent Reporting fromBeijing and GuiyangAt 37, Wang Zhu
body: Figure caption, Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scamsByLaura BickerChina correspondent Reporting fromBeijing and GuiyangAt 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts.They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman."The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you."So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate.He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married.Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over."My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head.He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie.She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age.He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches."My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chinese brides are in huge demand because of a steep gender imbalanceWang's story is an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis that has long been in the making in China.For decades, China's Communist Party decreed that couples could have only one child. They reversed course in January 2016 but by then the "one-child" policy, coupled with a preference for boys, had produced a shrinking pool of women and a stark gender imbalance.There are now 30 million more men than women in China – that's more than the male population of the UK, or the entire population of Australia.This has left men like Wang, who are in their late 30s and who live in smaller cities or far- flung, rural areas, with few options. Women in these places can afford to be choosy as they know they are in demand."The requirements for men are very high in my city. You need to have a car, a house and your family should preferably run a business," he says.Many families also demand a high "bride price", a longstanding Chinese custom where the groom's family gives money to the bride. In parts of China, where men far outnumber women, this has become a significant financial burden.Hence the appeal of matchmaking agencies like the ones in Guizhou, which are proposing a one-stop, quick solution - or "flash marriages".Matchmaking agencies are hardly new in China, but many seem to be finding vulnerable targets in men who are struggling to find partners as they grow older.So much so that state media recently reported that the industry had seen "rapid growth" which  had "bred illegal practices and chaos".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The "flash marriage" market is now on Beijing's radarIt's hard to determine the scale of such fraud across China but it has grown enough to draw the attention of Chinese officials. Between January 2024 and March 2025, prosecutors handled cases involving 1,546 individuals for crimes related to the matchmaking industry.This month, five separate authorities jointly launched a nationwide crackdown on the matchmaking industry after the issue generated "widespread public concern".In one case, a matchmaking agency reportedly used karaoke waitresses as bait to defraud 128 victims of more than 2.5 million yuan (£274,000, $371,000)."I think the government could introduce industry-specific regulations targeting flash marriage scams," Fan Binghe, from the Nanjing Office of the Beijing Jingshi law firm, told the BBC.Although Guiyang has become synonymous with this booming "flash marriage" market, there is little to suggest it is a romantic hub.The agency offices sit in a dense warren of buildings above a shopping precinct, where vendors sell local fruit and workers queue for takeaway sour soup rice noodles.Wang, however, was convinced he could trust them after the company told him they would do a full background check and that he would be entitled to compensation if he was the victim of fraud.So he paid up and the introductions began.Image caption, Wang was drawn to Guiyang by the promise of a demure spouse He met seven women in various "blind date" rooms over a few days while being carefully supervised by agency staff. He asked questions about where they came from, if they'd been married before and if they had any kids.He set his heart on the eighth woman he met. He was hoping to meet someone who hadn't been married before, with no children and who was just a little younger than him."She also dressed very simply," he recalls. "She looked introverted and honest."They met four or five times for just eight to ten minutes each time. He says they had been under strict instructions not to exchange phone numbers or any details on private messages, or they would be fined.After two or three days he decided she was the one and he agreed to pay her a substantial bride price. "I spent more than 300,000 yuan ($44,000)," he says, with a pile of well-thumbed legal papers in hand to prove it."If you include the wedding banquet and everything else, I spent around 400,000 to 500,000 yuan."The whole process was documented by the matchmaking agency in a series of glossy photos, which they also use to advertise their services on Chinese social media. In the video the couple are holding hands on a red carpet and smiling while romantic music plays in the background.Image caption, Wang with his ex-wife in a photo taken soon after their wedding  Just months into the marriage, debt collectors started calling, alleging she owed them money.Wang grew suspicious and wanted to know what else she had kept hidden. He checked her phone and found details of her former life, her birth certificate and former marriage documents.When he confronted her, she offered him a divorce, but refused to return a single penny of the bride price.He says he tried to hunt down the agency responsible for his marriage, but when he returned to their offices, they had packed up and disappeared.From his rented flat in Guiyang, just across from the main district which houses most of these agencies, Wang now spends his time making social media videos trying to warn other men about what can go wrong.In Guiyang, it is difficult to find an agency where the staff is willing to talk. One agency boss agreed to talk to us in their offices – although his business partner later asked us to leave.Inside there was a red carpet littered with fake petals ready for a proposal. He told us a couple had pledged to marry just hours before we arrived."There's a huge market for flash marriages in China. It only really emerged over the last two or three years," he told us.The agencies claim families here did not strictly adhere to the one-child policy, which means the area has a larger pool of women. "Even if a family had two or three daughters, they would keep trying for a son," one of them told the BBC.They say they are now trying to match these women with men from central provinces – like Wang who lives in Hebei – who are relatively wealthy but have few women around them."Our clients are free to choose whoever they like. The purpose of our business is to help people find someone they genuinely want to be with."One of the advertisements assures their prospective clients that "Three days with the right introduction can beat three years of dating".Image caption, It was in a room like this where Wang met his brideWang now spends his time trying to help other victims of similar spiels.His rented flat is full of men who are either searching for the owners of the agency who scammed them, or are trying to recoup their losses from their wives who ran off after only a few weeks of marriage.On a fold-up bed by the window, 59-year-old Xu Rulin from Jiangxi province pulls his carefully collated evidence out of a red plastic shopping bag.He spent nearly 500,000 yuan trying to find his son a wife through a "flash marriage" agency.Together they travelled to Guiyang - more than 1,000km away - and his son wed just seven days after he first met his bride in a "blind date" room.Xu says after the marriage was registered, she demanded they buy her an iPhone and transfer around 20,000 yuan to help her with her business. She also asked for 120,000 yuan for a wedding dress and jewellery, he claims."All I wanted was for her to genuinely settle down and live with us," he told us. "She said she wanted a house and I agreed to buy one for them. It was all agreed."But he says she ran away after living with them for less than two weeks. She has been detained by the police, and the couple have been able to get divorced.He says the owners of the matchmaking company were also arrested in January this year, but he is still in Guiyang trying to recover some of the losses.Image caption, The bride Xu Rulin spent a fortune finding for his son ran away within two weeksThe agency manager the BBC spoke to admitted there were no formal background checks on their clients."The women are introduced by local matchmakers who already know them very well. They know their family background because they're often from the same village. The male's matchmaker also usually knows the man very well."They would not say how much their services cost because that information was "confidential".He did say that if the information provided by either side is not truthful, then the client is entitled to get their money back."I'd say more than 90% of what our clients tell us here is true," he claimed."We have a saying here in China. One rotten mouse dropping spoils the whole pot of soup. That's exactly what it's like. We regularly attend meetings with the local police. If a matchmaking agency is found to be involved in marriage fraud, it will be held legally responsible."Image caption, This matchmaker says most people in the industry are genuineThis brings little comfort for those who have lost whatever money they had saved."I never imagined that with the agency charging such a high service fee, a local matchmaker in her hometown checking her background and the company offering so many guarantees, that the women's information would turn out to be completely fake," Wang says.He is almost resigned now to his losses. And he blames himself for falling for the scam: "Only women with problems would agree to these kind of flash marriages."He has kneeled at the police offices in Guiyang pleading for them to help him get his money back and he has even travelled to Beijing to urge the authorities to do more to combat this type of crime.These cases are difficult to prosecute, says Fan Binghe, the lawyer who has handled many.For one, Chinese law has no specific criminal offence which covers this kind of marriage fraud, and so to bring criminal charges, a victim has to establish that the aim of their spouse was always to take their money."In cases I've handled, suspects often argue that they genuinely intended to marry and live a good life but realised they were incompatible, had conflicts, and decided to end the relationship," he says."In situations like that, the line becomes blurred. Relationship issues are difficult to disprove."Image caption, Wang's apartment has turned into a refuge for scammed menEven harder is getting money back from sham matchmaking agencies which often shut up shop as soon as they have made enough cash.Wang has managed to get some money back, but not all."After going through something like this, I don't even know if I can still get married. It was already hard for me to find someone. And now I've spent so much money. I won't consider it now."Wang's life, and the life of the men in the apartment, all appear to be in limbo."It has taken almost two years, and even now I still don't know when I can divorce her," he says, surrounded by his legal paperwork."I don't know when this will be resolved, so I can restart a normal life. It feels endless."

title: Michael Sheen investigates cancer concern around chemical dumping
description: What he told me made my blood run cold - Michael Sheen investigates Wales' toxic legacyImage source, Wall to Wall MediaImage caption, Michael Sheen in
body: What he told me made my blood run cold - Michael Sheen investigates Wales' toxic legacyImage source, Wall to Wall MediaImage caption, Michael Sheen investigates Wales' toxic legacy in a new BBC iPlayer documentary ByRowenna HoskinBBC Wales and Steffan MessengerWales environment correspondentMichael Phillips spent his childhood in the 1980s playing with friends at a lagoon, firing air guns at rusty barrels that released clouds of coloured powder - completely oblivious to the toxic chemicals within.Decades later, several of those friends and Phillips himself have developed rare cancers, which they believe may be linked to this.Researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan tried to sound the alarm about 14 such sites - 12 of which were in Wales - but died before his warnings were heeded. "What he told me made my blood run cold," said Hollywood actor Michael Sheen, who spoke to Gowan just months before he died and has now continued his investigation in a new BBC iPlayer documentary.Gowan, a former farming consultant, alleged that chemical giant Monsanto had dumped "huge amounts of industrial chemicals all around Wales".These included polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), he said, which he described as "some of the worst contaminants known to man" and were widely used during the last century, including for lipsticks and white goods."This stuff builds up in the environment, builds up in animals and fish, and it builds up in us," Gowan said.Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond to either Sheen and his team or the BBC when asked to comment.Image caption, Douglas Gowan spent half a century trying to make people listen to his concerns about chemical contamination in WalesSheen said PCBs were now known as "the godfather of forever chemicals". He added: "There is something out there in the forest, there is something in our bodies that can turn against us and tear us apart, but it's not like it is in the horror films. It's invisible. It's a silent killer."These manmade chemicals are stable, resistant to extreme temperatures and pressures and have insulating properties. Because of this they were used in everything from plastics and paint to electrical equipment.After concerns about toxicity to humans and animals were raised, a series of bans were put in place around the world from the 1970s onwards.But the chemicals take a long time to break down and have lingered in the environment, particularly in landfill, where they can leach into waterways and then into the sea.Gowan told Sheen in the documentary: "There was no regulation at the time, they could dump it wherever they wanted to."Image source, BBC/Wall to Wall MediaImage caption, Archive footage shows a blaze at Llwyneinion near Ruabon in Wrexham, where the effects of the chemicals were reportedly felt up to 20 miles awayIn the 1980s, a fire at the lagoon at Llwyneinion near Ruabon in Wrexham took 60 firefighters more than 18 hours to bring under control.The effects of the chemicals were reportedly felt up to 20 miles (32km) away.Phillips and his friends went to watch and he believes the impact of this exposure began to emerge in 2001."I started getting lumps on my shoulder, I caught cancer. I lost a large part of my shoulder that's literally as wide as my hand."While he was operating, my surgeon said 'this is strange, I've never seen this type of cancer before', and he'd had a distinguished career of 40 years." Image source, BBC/Wall to Wall MediaImage caption, Michael Phillips played at the lagoon near Ruabon as a child and believes it has had a devastating impact on his lifeIt was not just him who was affected. "I lost a very close friend who used to be [at the lagoon] all the time, more than me. He died of breast cancer."I have another friend who passed away with brain cancer. I've got another friend who is trying to get over brain cancer, I have another friend who's had all of his lymph glands taken out because they were cancerous." Another friend has the exact type of cancer Phillips had, and his surgeon told him: "For me to catch what I had was like winning the lottery."For your friend who lives down the road to get exactly the same, he said it's like winning the lottery every day for six months. It's not a coincidence." Phillips' blood tests showed higher-than-average PCB levels. "It's chilling to think that having any PCBs in your blood is normal, when 90 years ago no-one would have had them as they didn't exist," said Sheen.The actor also had his blood tested and it revealed 81 different types of PCBs, despite him not having lived near any dump sites. "There is no safe level of PCBs, it's a risk all of us have to try and manage. The lower your level of PCBs, the lower your risk of getting cancer," he said.Image source, BBC/Wall to Wall MediaImage caption, Paul Pemberton has been a councillor for more than 20 yearsPaul Pemberton has been a Wrexham councillor for more than 20 years and said the site had been "abused for many many years". Scientists found cyanide, arsenic and PCBs at the site and said it needed to be cleaned up, he said.  "We were then quoted around about £45m and that would bankrupt the council," he said.However, Wrexham council said later investigations and risk assessments concluded that although contaminants were present, the sites did not meet the legal threshold requiring remediation.In 2017, Gowan said the companies responsible "should be made to remediate".Image source, BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Aled JenkinsImage caption, Sheen met one of the US attorneys who helped a town sue MonsantoWales was not Monsanto's first choice when it came to PCB dumping.Initially it pumped PCBs into waterways in Anniston, Alabama. In 1993, the whole town sued Monsanto for chemical contamination, resulting in one of the largest single town lawsuits in US history. Donald Stewart, one of the attorneys involved, said it was settled for $300m.Internal Monsanto documents showed they had been aware of the toxicity of PCBs in 1949, so how could they get away with knowingly exposing people to these chemicals?Stewart said: "If you look at this area, it's working people. They were people who wouldn't be able to fight back." Image source, BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Stephen PerryImage caption, Journalists Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor received Gowan's folders of documents when he diedIn another memo from 1972, journalists Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor helping Sheen with the investigation found that Monsanto had decided PCBs were a worldwide problem, an environmental danger and a risk to human health, and were shutting down work at Anniston. But then there were proposals to increase capacity to make five million more kilograms of PCBs at their plant in Newport. "They're doing it in Newport because the legal risk in America is so much," said Ashby."Then the government in the UK told industry we're not going to put any restrictions on importing PCBs. So they begin importing from around the world, hundreds of tonnes of PCBs." Gowan said: "If one wanted to be cynical about it, you could say that almost they were choosing places where chronic health issues might be hidden behind pre-existing health issues."People grew up with the knowledge that... they were in an area that had coal mining, heavy industry, the environment was contaminated, and there were health problems."Image caption, There are 12 locations in Wales which were sites of concern for Douglas GowanSheen and his team took their findings to Wales' Parliament in the hope that more tests can be done. "These people deserve more," he said."They deserve their concerns to be met with proper research and appropriate action. Douglas spent most of his life fighting to get the truth out there."The fact we all have traces of this chemical in our blood shows that we all have skin in the game. We've got to get together, we've got to fight this." Meanwhile, members of the documentary team will appear before the Welsh Affairs Committee as it looks into alleged toxic "forever chemical" contamination in south Wales, the BBC has been told.Image source, BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Stephen PerryImage caption, Michael Sheen said he hopes international action is taken as Wales is not the only place that is affectedAt a screening of the documentary, Sheen said: "These are just the places we know about... Douglas Gowan believed that there was much more."Kirsty Luff of Friends of the Earth Cymru has called for a public inquiry into the "scale and impact of toxic sites in Wales".She warned that climate change would make the situation worse as "more frequent and intense flooding... will bring these contaminants to the surface where they can spread over fields, they can get into water courses".Image source, BBC/Wall to Wall Media/Stephen HartImage caption, Dr Dave Megson, an environmental chemist, sampled 14 sites, including 12 in WalesEnvironmental regulator Natural Resources Wales tested Llwyneinion acid tar lagoon close to Ruabon.Investigation work found the site did not meet the legal definition of contaminated land.Wrexham council said because of this there was "no statutory requirement for remediation", but that it continued to carry out regular inspections and water monitoring.It said only limited information from more recent testing had been shared with it, but it remained open to reviewing any new "robust and verifiable evidence".The Welsh government said: "Addressing contaminated land is a key priority for this government."Our industrial heritage has left us with a difficult legacy that can affect both people and places - we want to ensure this does not pose a risk to our communities or our natural environment."A survey of local authorities carried out by Natural Resources Wales in 2015 identified more than 9,000 potential sites requiring further investigation."While not all of these sites will pose a risk to human health or the environment, this figure demonstrates the scale of the issue facing regulators in Wales."We now intend to develop a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land, so that communities are no longer exposed to potential risks."Buried with Michael Sheen is on BBC Two, BBC One Wales and BBC iPlayer from 17 August at 21:00 BSTAdditional reporting by Steffan Messenger
