title: My brother was found dead – but police didn't realise for days that he had been shot
description: Image source, Douglas LowImage caption, Brian Low was murdered on a rural path near Aberfeldy in February 2024ByGraeme OgstonTayside and Central repor
body: Image source, Douglas LowImage caption, Brian Low was murdered on a rural path near Aberfeldy in February 2024ByGraeme OgstonTayside and Central reporterBrian Low was walking his dog on a remote country path when he was shot dead by a former colleague whose hatred had festered for years.The 65-year-old was found near Aberfeldy in Highland Perthshire with blood on his hands and face - but police did not realise at first that he had been murdered.The former groundsman's death was not treated as suspicious for several days, until a post-mortem confirmed he had died from gunshot wounds. Shotgun pellets had fallen from the body bag before his body was examined.It was another three months before the killer, retired gamekeeper David Campbell, was arrested.He is now serving life for murder - but Brian Low's family still cannot understand the mistakes which were made after his body was found.They have spoken publicly for the first time in two-part BBC documentary Murder Trial: Death of a Dog Walker, which follows the police investigation and the trial."I was so angry and so sad at the same time," says his brother Douglas Low."How could this happen?"Image source, Firecrest MediaImage caption, Brian Low's brother Douglas said he was angry and sad at the police blunderBrian Low's body was discovered on Leafy Lane, with his dog Millie by his side, on the morning of 17 February 2024.One of the first detectives on the scene told the murder trial that he believed Low's injuries were consistent with him falling while out for a walk.The court was shown graphic photographs of Low's body lying on the path. His face was covered in blood and black marks.Douglas Low said the pictures were "so horrific I barely kept my breakfast down. I can't imagine why someone would say that's a medical event".Brian's niece, Jacqui Low, added: "It just seems incredible that they didn't see the marks on his face, the shot."The post-mortem found that Low's clothes were peppered with holes and he had sustained about 30 pellet injuries.Image caption, A police cordon was not erected at the scene until days after Brian Low's deathThe delays meant that a cordon at the crime scene was not put in place until 23 February, six days after Low's body was found.Det Ch Insp Martin MacDougall, of the Major Investigation Team, said: "When you have that delay, a number of things go through your mind of what we could potentially have lost evidentially."Footprints in the soil, tyre tracks, CCTV."The murder inquiry was finally launched 10 days after Low's body was discovered.A press conference took place a few days later, where MacDougall and colleague Cdr Greg Burns were grilled over the blunder.One detective told the filmmakers that there had been a lot of media interest and admitted: "We're kind of a wee bit on the back foot".Murder Trial: Death of a Dog WalkerBrian Low is shot and found dead in rural Scotland. David Campbell, former gamekeeper of the shooting estate where he worked, stands accused of his premeditated murder.Over the next three months police spoke to 800 witnesses and trawled through 2,400 hours of CCTV footage from 56 cameras.The documentary followed prosecutor Greg Farrell as his team built the case against Campbell, as well as the accused's lawyer, Tony Lenehan KC, as he attempted to dismantle the prosecution's timeline and cast doubt on the evidence.Because of the potential missed forensic opportunities, the prosecution led a circumstantial case during the trial.It linked smaller strands of evidence to build a picture of Campbell's decades-old grudge against Low, who had worked at the nearby Edradynate Estate with his future killer for more than 20 years.Image source, Firecrest FilmsImage caption, David Campbell was jailed for a minimum of 19 years for murdering Brian LowCampbell had been the head gamekeeper at the estate.He was described by local farmer Sally Crystal as "highly respected" and a man who "ran a very, very good shoot".Crystal had first met Campbell during the 1987 shooting season.She said that when he first arrived he had been an excellent gamekeeper - but as his reputation grew, he became "very arrogant"."David started really misbehaving, the family (who ran Edradynate) started mistrusting him," said Crystal.Image source, Firecrest FilmsImage caption, Sally Crystal told the trial that David Campbell told her he "hated" Brian LowAsked during the trial how the two men got along, she said: "At first it wasn't noticeable, but as time went on there was a coldness."On at least one occasion I had been talking to Brian in the morning and David walked past me."He turned to me, angry because I was slightly late that morning and I'd still had time to talk to Brian."He walked away and he said I (expletive) loathe that man. I hate him."Pam Curran, who was Low's partner for 22 years, said everyone who met Brian liked him."I don't think he had a bad bone in his body," she said.Douglas Low said he had not thought that his brother had an enemy in the world."Who would want to harm Brian? He was the nicest, kindest person you could ever imagine," he said."It's just so unbelievable."However, the trial was told of bad blood between the two men.Campbell had suspected Low of "planting" items which were allegedly found during a raid on his then-home on the estate after alleged bird poisonings.Image source, Firecrest FilmsImage caption, The documentary includes footage of Campbell's arrest three months after the murderCampbell said he had not had any contact with Low since 2017 and that he did not know he had left Edradynate Estate until he saw it on television.Pam Curran said: "I knew they had a fall-out, a serious one because Dave was being investigated for poisoning birds of prey and it had happened more than once."And whatever Brian had said to the police really angered Dave and they had a right set-to."Brian wouldn't tell me the ins and outs of it, but I knew it was bad. Brian was really upset by it."Campbell was removed from Edradynate in early 2017 having worked there for more than 30 years.During the trial, defence advocate Lenehan noted that in the seven years since he had left the estate both men had lived near each other without there being any issue.But in reality, Campbell had been planning how to kill Low - and cover his tracks.Figure caption, Watch: David Campbell covers doorbell with duct tapeOn the morning of Friday 16 February 2024, Campbell set to work on his plan.He covered the CCTV camera at the rear of his home with duct tape in the morning, not removing it until that evening.A figure the prosecution said was Campbell was seen on CCTV riding through Aberfeldy on a distinctive bicycle, heading in the direction of the murder scene.One witness told the trial that Campbell had later asked a bike repair shop to change the tyres.The police also saw CCTV footage from a nearby farm showing a "spooked " horse running around a field, at the same time Low was believed to have been shot.Officers say the time matched the last known activity from Low's mobile phone.Image source, Firecrest FilmsImage caption, CCTV showed a horse in a nearby field that was "spooked" at the same time police believe Brian Low was shotThree months after the killing, police finally arrested Campbell.He was on the toilet naked when officers arrived at his home.In a combative police interview, Campbell was asked by arresting officer Det Con David Budd if Low's death had been an accident."I don't know," he replied.Budd asked him: "Well did you mean to shoot him or not?" - to which Campbell replied: "Cheeky bastard."He went on to say that he "100%" did not have anything to do with Brian Low's death.Image source, Firecrest MoviesImage caption, David Campbell's combative police interview is shown in the documentaryCampbell gave evidence in his own defence during the trial.He said he spent most of the day in his house and made a lengthy call to the local council about a planning application.Campbell said he did not ask for a solicitor after his arrest because he "didn't need one" and denied having anything to do with Low's death.However, he was found guilty of murder after a 15-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The jury delivered its verdict after three days of deliberations.Judge Lord Scott told Campbell his "targeted assassination" had been "an appalling and senseless act of extreme wickedness."He was jailed for life and ordered to serve a minimum of 19 years before he can apply for parole.Figure caption, Judge Lord Scott: 'You believed you had got away with murder'Pam Curran said she had not been able to go into court for the verdict because she did not know how she would react."That one act of violence has changed so many people's lives, and for what?"An argument over something on an estate that happened years ago."She said her life would never be the same."I'm not getting to see Brian ever again. How is that right?""But you can't feel sorry for yourself."You just have to pick yourself up and keep going, because that's what he would have wanted."

title: 'We've had a lot of close calls': Canada wildfire evacuees wonder if they still have homes
description: Figure caption, "That fire came so fast": Wildfire rages in British ColumbiaByNadine YousifSenior Canada reporter and Brandon DrenonBBC NewsEarl Kurz
body: Figure caption, "That fire came so fast": Wildfire rages in British ColumbiaByNadine YousifSenior Canada reporter and Brandon DrenonBBC NewsEarl Kurz and his wife have lived in Peachland, a town overlooking Okanagan Lake in Canada's British Columbia, for 30 years. In the last 10, he said he has grown used to wildfires threatening his community.But this is the first time he's been forced to flee, and surveying the damage left behind by the Bald Range wildfire, which broke out on Friday and grew in a matter of hours to 53 sq miles (136 sq km) in size, has been difficult."It's total incinerated destruction," Kurz said. "The hot spots are just barren areas of nothing except 12 inches of ash."Officials in British Columbia are still trying to determine how many homes were lost to the fire, which remains out of control as of Monday. More than 12,000 residents in the area are still under an evacuation order. One woman, aged 80, died while trying to flee from the wildfire, police said on Sunday.With dry lightning, high temperatures and winds in the forecast, officials warned on Monday that the fire continues to be a threat and that new ignitions are possible.The Okanagan area of British Columbia, known for its world renowned vineyards and picturesque scenery, has been grappling with extreme drought in recent years. As of July, the level of the Okanagan Lake was at its lowest since 1992, according to the Okanagan Basin Water Board.The Bald Range wildfire is one of more than 100 burning in British Columbia as of Monday - 70 of which started in the last week alone. The west coast province's premier, David Eby, declared a state of emergency over the weekend, urging residents to heed evacuation orders and warning that the fires continue to move "incredibly quickly".Image source, Supplied/Keegan RadomskiImage caption, Keegan Radomski's home, photographed here before the fire, was built by her grandmother in 1996. Keegan Radomski is one of thousands who have had to flee their homes in Summerland, a town on the Okanagan Lake just south of Peachland. The 18-year-old told the BBC she barely escaped with her mother's ashes before she saw the fire breach her property."We've had a lot of close calls before, but it's never been like this," Radomski said. "You always think it's not going to be you, and then it's you."The home she fled was built by her grandmother 30 years ago, she said. Living in the Okanagan for decades meant that Radomski and her family are familiar with wildfires and evacuation notices, but they were still caught off guard by the speed of this fire. The family noticed wildfire smoke from the distance while eating dinner on Friday evening. Less than four hours later, Radomski said she was scrambling to get everyone out as she saw a hill on her property begin to burn. She added she is still unsure if her family's home survived, and when she can return and check for herself.Image source, Supplied by Keegan RadomskiImage caption, Radomski says she is unsure of when she is able to return to her property and assess the damageDoug Holmes, the mayor of Summerland, told CBC News on Monday that some people's homes have been lost, but "we don't know how many"."I think we need to prepare for the fact that everybody is going to know somebody that has lost a home," Holmes said.Some residents in the farming community were forced to leave their livestock behind in the quick evacuation, said Kaz Nowlin, who has been helping rescue stranded animals in the Okanagan area since wildfires broke out last month. Nowlin said he and a group of volunteers have so far rescued dozens of animals, including 57 horses. He told the BBC he is in the process of acquiring a permit to enter Summerland and round up 14 alpacas and eight horses that have remained. "It's for the animals' well-being," he said of his efforts. "They don't deserve what's going on."Image source, Supplied by Kaz NowlinImage caption, Dozens of horses have been rescued by a volunteer group in and around the Okanagan Valley since wildfires broke out last month. The Bald Range wildfire comes on the heels of another fire in the Okanagan, called Bradley Creek, which is believed to have destroyed more than 200 homes.Officials said the Bradley Creek fire is now being held after "tireless work" by wildfire crews to contain it. Drought conditions have also contributed to fires in the US state of Washington, just south of British Columbia, where more than 65,000 people were forced to flee their homes. Devastating fires have also burned this summer in Spain and France as Europe grapples with drought and record high temperatures. France has seen its worst fires in two decades, while officials in the Spanish capital Madrid say theirs are the worst the region has ever experienced.Fires are part of the natural cycle of Canada's vast boreal forest, but experts say climate change - particularly hotter and dryer weather - has made them more intense and frequent in the last decade. In 2023, the country saw its worst wildfire season in history in terms of the total area burned.

title: Vandals target Halewood play park before it has even opened

body: "There is absolutely no reasoning behind this kind of mindless behaviour, but the impact is significant," he said."The cost to repair the equipment, remove the paint and assess any safety implications or wider damage will run into thousands of pounds."He said the facilities were due to open in time for local families to make the most of the park during the summer holidays and this would now have to be delayed due to the actions of a small number of people.Morgan said the incident had been reported to Merseyside Police and CCTV from the area was being reviewed "to find those responsible and ensure they understand the impact of their actions".The new facilities include separate junior and toddler play areas connected via a sensory path. A council spokesperson said new equipment suitable for ages 0-14 had been installed in recent weeks including new swings, slides, climbing frames, accessible and inclusive equipment and sensory panels.
